item.title: CONTEST UPDATE
item.content:encoded:
After receiving feedback from several users directly (and from observing draft discussions), I've decided to tweak the rules for this contest a bit.

Authors may now use just one SCP for their tale if they want. You are free to use more than one if you so choose, but you are no longer required to use two SCPs minimum.

As this edit to the rules came rather late, I'm extending the deadline a week so people who were previously struggling with their tales can have a bit of breathing room.

To the two authors who posted under the old rule set, thank you very much for doing so, and your tales are still going to be part of the competition. However, I understand this wasn't very fair for you, changing the rules so late in the game, so if you need to yell at me in a PM or a chat message, feel free.

item.content:encoded:
I would appreciate more explanation. Regardless of whether or not the 2000 contest was a "half-baked mess," what was wrong with its design? Even if it was launched early, how did this affect its functionality as a fair contest? What actually went wrong?

In regards to the 1000 anecdote, like I said in the original post, we are solving this problem by introducing a second, arbitrary force (people would have had to visit moose's article again to vote on it and he'd inevitably lose votes) to counterbalance the first one (he got votes quickly). This ignores what seems to be the perfectly fine solution from 2000, because like I said, everybody had an equal opportunity to write their entry in a reasonable amount of time and then post it simultaneously, which solves the first arbitrary influence, and obviously once you read an entry you could immediately vote on it, solving the second problem. This reminds me of myself in a high school chemistry lab where I fucked up one way and then I fucked up another way and then I crossed my fingers and prayed to God that the results would come out okay.

probably not an optimal solution

…upon further thought, i'm pretty sure that older contests were structured like this one (i wouldn't know because i didn't participate) and we made 2000 the way it was to fight the problems i've just listed?

Nope. The SCP-2000 contest was a half-baked mess that only half-solved the issues of previous contests because certain admins who will go unnamed pulled the trigger on it prematurely. This one had input from the technical team, and I believe it's a system that's worth trying.

Previous contests simply had everyone post their articles and then they were up for voting immediately. SCP-1000 was won literally weeks before the contest was over because everyone else didn't feel they could compete with moose's extremely high score.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
hey, question. Why are we having it such that voting is closed on posted articles until a certain time? Why aren't we using the same structure as the 2000 contest?

For the 2000 contest, it didn't matter how long it took you to write your article so long as you did it within the deadline, because you could only post your article at a certain point in time. this meant everyone got the opportunity for approximately equal viewing time. I can see two problems with this contest structure. The first one is that people who write faster get more viewing time, but how fast you can write shouldn't win you a contest. If contestant A and contestant B produce two works of exactly equal quality but A did it faster, does this mean that A is a better writer? …probably not.

Second, I guess there's another arbitrary force to counteract the first arbitrary force that I just mentioned. So if contestant A writes faster and posts an article sooner, while A gets more viewing time, A also gets screwed. A's article gets most of its views immediately after it's posted; anybody who's ever written an article knows that most of your votes come in, like, the week after you post. But people can't vote on A's article, so they'll just be like, "oh yeah I'll totally vote on this when voting opens," and maybe most of them will, but some of them won't. This happened in the 2000 contest too—people were like, "yeah, I'll vote on this when the contest ends," which was bizarre and silly, and then they didn't even vote, which demonstrates the problem. But the 2000 contest did not structurally require that people go back to articles that they liked and then vote on them.

So at the end of the day, if Contestant A is a faster writer, they'll get more pageviews, which they probably shouldn't, but also get screwed in the voting, which they probably shouldn't, and I guess we're crossing our fingers and hoping that those two things cancel out? What was wrong with the 2000 contest structure?

edit: to elaborate more on the "faster contestant" issue—in the 2000 contest, if Eskobar or Faminepulse had posted their articles at the same time as FFB's, who knows what would have happened? unlike the 2000 contest, this contest has that problem inherent in its structure.

…upon further thought, i'm pretty sure that older contests were structured like this one (i wouldn't know because i didn't participate) and we made 2000 the way it was to fight the problems i've just listed?
